question: Using elementary row transformations, examine whether the matrix $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\2&3&5\\3&4&7\end{bmatrix}$$ can be transformed into the identity matrix, and hence determine whether $A^{-1}$ exists.
explanation:
Applying Row Transformations

Start with $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\2&3&5\\3&4&7\end{bmatrix}$$ Apply $$R_2\to R_2-2R_1$$ to obtain $$\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\0&1&1\\3&4&7\end{bmatrix}$$ Next apply $$R_3\to R_3-3R_1$$ giving $$\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\0&1&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}$$ Now apply $$R_3\to R_3-R_2$$ We obtain $$\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}$$

Existence of the Inverse

The transformations have produced a row consisting entirely of zeros. Such a row cannot be converted by elementary row transformations into the corresponding row of the identity matrix. Hence, the given matrix cannot be transformed into $I_3$. Therefore, an inverse matrix cannot be obtained for $A$.

Final Result

The matrix $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\2&3&5\\3&4&7\end{bmatrix}$$ is not invertible, and hence $$A^{-1}$$ does not exist.

options.A: $A$ can be transformed into $I_3$, so $A^{-1}$ exists
options.B: Row reduction produces a zero row, so $A$ cannot be transformed into $I_3$ and $A^{-1}$ does not exist
options.C: Row reduction produces $I_3$ after one additional row interchange, so $A^{-1}$ exists
options.D: The matrix is already equivalent to $I_3$ without producing any zero row, so $A^{-1}$ exists
